questions.prompt: How is measurement defined in the lecture?

options.text: The empirical objective assignment of values to entities to characterize a specific attribute
The subjective ranking of software quality
Counting only the lines of code

questions.explanation: Measurement is the process of empirical objective assignment of values to entities in order to characterize a specific attribute thereof.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes a base measure from a derived measure?

options.text: A base measure is collected directly; a derived measure is computed from other measures
A base measure is always subjective
A derived measure cannot use base measures

questions.explanation: A base measure is collected directly by interacting with the entity; a derived measure is computed on the basis of other measures (e.g. productivity = LOC/effort).

questions.prompt: Which is an example of an external measure?
questions.explanation: External measures depend on how the entity relates to its environment (e.g. reliability); internal measures depend only on the entity itself (e.g. source code length).

questions.prompt: Which of the following are measurement scale types described by Stevens?
questions.explanation: The scale types are Nominal, Ordinal, Interval, Ratio, and Absolute, classified by their set of admissible transformations.

questions.prompt: On which scale does the ratio between two values become meaningful because a true zero exists?
questions.explanation: A ratio scale has a true zero (total lack of the attribute), so ratios are meaningful; admissible transformations are M' = a·M with a>0. On interval scales ratios make no sense.

questions.prompt: The statement 'The temperature in Tokyo is twice that in London' is meaningful on the Celsius scale.
questions.explanation: Temperature in Celsius/Fahrenheit is an interval scale (no true zero), so a 'twice as much' ratio statement is not invariant under admissible transformations — it is not meaningful.

questions.prompt: For a typical (non-strongly-connected) control flow graph, how is McCabe's cyclomatic number computed?
questions.explanation: For a strongly connected graph V(G) = #E − #N + 1; a typical CFG isn't strongly connected, so V(G) = #E − #N + 2 (the number of linearly independent paths).

questions.prompt: Which are Chidamber & Kemerer (CK) object-oriented design metrics?
questions.explanation: CK metrics include WMC, NOC, DIT, CBO, RFC, and LCOM; LOC is a separate size metric, not part of CK.

questions.prompt: Which law states 'When a measure becomes a target it ceases to be a good measure'?
questions.explanation: Goodhart's law: when a measure becomes a target it ceases to be a good measure. Campbell's law is the related warning about corruption of social indicators.

questions.prompt: In the SMART criteria for indicators, what does the 'M' stand for?
questions.explanation: SMART indicators are Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, and Timely.

questions.prompt: Which are the three entity categories in software measurement?
questions.explanation: Entities are categorized as Resource (input to a process), Process (an activity/event), and Product (an object/service resulting from a process).

questions.prompt: Which statistics are meaningful on a nominal scale?

options.text: Frequency per category and the mode

questions.explanation: Nominal scales support only counting, so the available statistics are frequency per category and the mode (no ordering or mean).

questions.prompt: Lines of Code is easy to understand but hard to measure precisely, and using it for productivity does not favor well-structured programs.
questions.explanation: LOC is intuitive and widely used but hard to measure precisely; if used to measure productivity it does not reward well-structured programs.

questions.prompt: In one common classification of McCabe's cyclomatic complexity, what does a value of 1–10 indicate?
questions.explanation: A common CC classification: 1–10 low-risk, 11–20 moderate risk, 21–50 high risk, and >50 most complex and highly unstable.

questions.prompt: Function Point Analysis was originally developed by whom?
questions.explanation: Function Point Analysis was developed by Allan J. Albrecht in the late 1970s; variations include COSMIC, IFPUG, Mk II, NESMA, and FiSMA.

questions.prompt: Which law warns that the more a quantitative indicator is used for decision-making, the more it will be subject to corruption pressures?
questions.explanation: Campbell's law: the more any quantitative social indicator is used for decision-making, the more it is subject to corruption and the more it distorts the processes it monitors.

questions.prompt: What set of admissible transformations defines an ordinal scale?
questions.explanation: An ordinal scale preserves order, so its admissible transformations are all monotonic increasing functions; meaningful statistics include the median and quantiles.

questions.prompt: Which two problems does measurement theory formally address?

options.text: The representation problem (axioms/conditions under which measurement is possible)
The uniqueness problem (how unique the measure or scale is)

questions.explanation: Measurement theory (Stevens, 1946) addresses the representation problem (prescriptive conditions for measurement) and the uniqueness problem (descriptive: how unique the scale is).

questions.prompt: Which operations are meaningful on an interval scale?

options.text: Addition and subtraction make sense, but the ratio does not (admissible transformations are affine: M' = a·M + b)
Ratios are meaningful because there is a true zero

questions.explanation: Interval scales preserve order and differences, so addition/subtraction make sense but ratios do not; admissible transformations are affine (M' = a·M + b), e.g. temperature/relative time.

questions.prompt: What characterizes an absolute scale?

options.text: Measurement by counting items, with only one possible mapping (M' = M)

questions.explanation: An absolute scale measures by counting items; only one mapping is possible (M' = M) and all arithmetic is meaningful (e.g. number of full-time developers).

questions.prompt: In COSMIC Function Points, which are the four data movement types?

options.text: Read and Write (between system and persistent storage)

questions.explanation: COSMIC FP data movements are Entry, Exit, Read, and Write; each functional process is started by its triggering Entry data movement.

questions.prompt: What does the CK metric 'Response For a Class' (RFC) count?

options.text: The methods in the class plus the remote methods directly called by them
The maximum inheritance depth to the root
The pairs of methods sharing attributes

questions.explanation: RFC is the sum of the class's methods plus the remote methods directly called by them; NOC counts subclasses, DIT is inheritance depth, and LCOM relates to method/attribute sharing.
